name: Calf stretch, straight knee
why: Stretches the big upper calf muscle (gastrocnemius). A tight calf adds strain to the Achilles, the arch of the foot and the inside of the ankle.
setup: Stand facing a wall with your hands on it.
Step one foot back, heel down and toes pointing straight forward.
cues: Lean in until the calf stretches
feel: A stretch in the upper part of the back calf.
stopIf: Sharp pain in the heel, Achilles or ankle.

name: Calf stretch, bent knee
why: Bending the knee shifts the stretch to the deeper, lower calf muscle (soleus), which works hard in running and walking downhill.
setup: Stand facing a wall with your hands on it, one foot a short step behind the other.
Keep both heels down.
cues: Sink until the low calf stretches
feel: A stretch low in the calf, just above the heel.
stopIf: Sharp pain in the heel, Achilles or ankle.

name: Plantar fascia stretch
why: Stretches the thick band under your foot (plantar fascia). Doing it before your first steps in the morning reduces that sharp first-step heel pain.
setup: Sit and cross the sore foot over your other knee.
cues: Pull your toes back towards your shin
Feel the band under the arch tighten
mistakes: Pulling the ankle instead of the toes
feel: A stretch along the arch and into the heel.
stopIf: Sharp heel pain.
references: DiGiovanni BF, et al. 2003. Tissue-specific plantar fascia-stretching exercise enhances outcomes in patients with chronic heel pain. J Bone Joint Surg Am 85:1270-7.

name: Short foot (arch lift)
why: Trains the small muscles that lift your arch, supporting the foot when the arch tends to flatten. Progress to doing it standing, then on one leg.
setup: Sit with your feet flat on the floor.
cues: Slide the ball of the foot towards the heel
Keep your toes long and relaxed
mistakes: Rolling onto the outside of the foot
feel: Effort in the arch of the foot.
stopIf: Cramping that doesn't ease, or arch pain.

media.credit: Video: Short Foot Exercise (Singapore General Hospital)

name: Ankle inversion hold (isometric)
why: Pressing the inside of the foot against something solid works the tibialis posterior, the tendon on the inside of the ankle that holds up your arch, without moving the ankle. A gentle starting point when that tendon is painful.
setup: Sit with both feet flat on the floor.
Place the inside edge of the working foot against the inside of your other foot, or a table leg.
feel: Effort along the inside of the ankle and lower shin.
stopIf: Sharp pain on the inside of the ankle.

name: Resisted ankle inversion (band)
why: Strengthens the tibialis posterior through its full movement, with a slow lowering phase that tendons respond well to. Resisted exercise like this is part of non-surgical treatment for posterior tibial tendon problems.
setup: Sit with the working leg crossed over the other knee, or with the foot flat on the floor.
Loop a band around the forefoot and hold or anchor it to the outside, so it pulls the foot outwards.
Keep your toes pointed slightly down: this targets the tendon on the inside of the ankle best.
cues: Turn the sole of your foot inwards
Move from the ankle, not the knee
mistakes: Rotating the whole leg instead of the foot
Using a band that's too heavy
feel: Work along the inside of the ankle and lower shin.
stopIf: Sharp pain on the inside of the ankle, or it's more painful the next morning.
references: Kulig K, et al. 2009. Nonsurgical management of posterior tibial tendon dysfunction with orthoses and resistive exercise: a randomized controlled trial. Phys Ther 89:26-37.

media.credit: Video: Rehab exercise; Tibialis Posterior; Banded Plantarflexed Adduction (Liam Stapleton (Podiatric Sports Medicine))

name: Heel raise (both legs)
why: Builds calf and Achilles strength for walking, running and hiking. The first step before single-leg raises.
setup: Stand with your fingertips on a wall, feet hip-width apart.
cues: Rise up onto the balls of your feet
mistakes: Rolling out onto the little toes
feel: Work in the calves.
stopIf: Sharp pain in the heel, Achilles or ankle.

name: Heel raise with ball squeeze
why: Rising onto your toes while squeezing something between your heels makes the tibialis posterior, the tendon that holds up your arch, work harder. Building its strength is the core of rehab for posterior tibial tendon problems.
setup: Stand facing a wall or counter with your fingertips on it for balance.
Place a small soft ball or rolled-up towel between your ankles, just above the heels.
cues: Rise up through the big toe
mistakes: Rolling out onto the little toes
feel: Work in the calves and along the inside of the ankles and arches.
stopIf: Sharp pain on the inside of the ankle, or the ankle feels unstable.

media.credit: Video: Heel Raise With Ball Squeeze - For Posterior Tib Activation (Sole Physical Therapy)

name: Single-leg heel raise

defaultDose.load: Add a backpack when 3 x 15 is easy

why: The benchmark for calf, Achilles and posterior tibial tendon strength. Being able to do 20 or more on each leg is a good sign you're ready to run.
setup: Stand on one foot with fingertips on a wall for balance only.
cues: Rise as high as you can
Keep your weight over the big toe
mistakes: Rolling onto the outside of the foot
feel: Hard work in the calf of the standing leg.
stopIf: Sharp pain in the heel, Achilles or inside of the ankle.

media.credit: Video: Single Leg Heel Raises - Ask Doctor Jo (AskDoctorJo)

name: Single-leg balance
why: Trains the ankle, foot and hip muscles to react and keep your arch and knee steady. Important after ankle problems and for uneven trails. Harder: close your eyes or stand on a cushion.
setup: Stand on one leg near a wall or counter, knee slightly soft.
cues: Touch the wall only if you need to
mistakes: Hip dropping on the lifted side
feel: Small muscles in the foot, ankle and hip working.
stopIf: Ankle pain.
cautions: Stay near support if your balance is poor.

media.credit: Video: Single Leg Balance - Increase Ankle Strength and Stability (Center For Total Back Care)

name: Toe raise against a wall
why: Strengthens the muscle at the front of the shin, which helps control landing and can protect against shin pain in runners and hikers.
setup: Stand with your back and bottom against a wall, heels about 30 cm out from it.
cues: Lift your toes towards your shins
feel: Work at the front of the shins.
stopIf: Sharp shin pain.

name: Pogo hops
why: Small, springy hops train the calf and Achilles to store and release energy like springs, preparing them for running.
setup: Stand tall, feet hip-width apart.
cues: Small quick hops on the balls of your feet
feel: Springy work in the calves.
stopIf: Pain in the Achilles, shin, heel or inside of the ankle.
cautions: Only once you can do 3 x 15 single-leg heel raises without pain.

media.credit: Video: Pogo Hops (Drs. Mike & Kelly Swann)

name: High-load heel raise (towel under toes)

defaultDose.load: Add a backpack with books as it gets easier

why: Rising slowly on one leg with the toes bent up over a rolled towel loads the plantar fascia and calf heavily. Done every other day and progressed over weeks, this kind of strength training helps plantar heel pain.
setup: Stand on a step on the sore foot, a rolled towel under your toes so they're bent up.
Let the heel hang off the edge; hold a rail or wall for balance only.
mistakes: Using both feet when it's meant to be one
feel: Hard work in the calf and a strong stretch-load under the foot.
stopIf: Sharp heel pain that stays, or the heel is clearly worse the next morning.
cautions: Every other day, not daily: the tissue needs recovery time.
references: Rathleff MS, et al. 2015. High-load strength training improves outcome in patients with plantar fasciitis: a randomized controlled trial with 12 months follow-up. Scand J Med Sci Sports 25:e292-300.

name: Heel drop off a step, straight knee

defaultDose.load: Add a backpack when it's easy

why: Slowly lowering your body weight on one leg loads the Achilles tendon in the way it adapts to best. A classic, well-tested treatment for pain in the middle of the tendon.
setup: Stand on the edge of a step on the balls of both feet, holding a rail or wall.
Rise up on both feet, then shift your weight onto the sore leg.
cues: Lower the heel slowly below the step
mistakes: Rising up on the sore leg (rise on both)
Bending the knee in this version
feel: Hard work and a stretch in the calf and Achilles. Some tendon discomfort is OK.
stopIf: Pain above about 5 out of 10, or it's worse the next morning.
cautions: For pain where the tendon joins the heel bone, don't drop below the step: use heel raises on flat ground instead.
references: Alfredson H, et al. 1998. Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. Am J Sports Med 26:360-6.

name: Heel drop off a step, bent knee

defaultDose.load: Add a backpack when it's easy

why: The bent-knee version of the heel drop works the deeper calf muscle (soleus) and the Achilles.
setup: Stand on the edge of a step on the balls of both feet, holding a rail or wall.
Bend your knees a little and keep them bent throughout.
cues: Shift onto the sore leg, knee bent
feel: Work low in the calf and in the Achilles. Some tendon discomfort is OK.
stopIf: Pain above about 5 out of 10, or it's worse the next morning.
cautions: For pain where the tendon joins the heel bone, don't drop below the step.
references: Alfredson H, et al. 1998. Heavy-load eccentric calf muscle training for the treatment of chronic Achilles tendinosis. Am J Sports Med 26:360-6.

name: Calf raise hold (isometric)
why: Holding a half-height heel raise loads the calf and Achilles without moving: a gentle way to keep the tendon working when it's painful.
setup: Stand on the sore leg on flat ground, fingertips on a wall.
feel: Steady work in the calf.
stopIf: Pain above about 3-4 out of 10.

name: Single-leg heel raise, bent knee
why: Strengthens the soleus, the deep calf muscle that takes huge loads in running. Weak soleus muscles are common with shin and Achilles pain.
setup: Stand on one leg with the knee slightly bent, fingertips on a wall.
cues: Rise as high as you can
mistakes: Straightening the knee as you rise
Rolling to the outside of the foot
feel: Work low in the calf.
stopIf: Sharp pain in the shin, Achilles or heel.

name: Ankle alphabet
why: Moving the ankle gently in every direction soon after a sprain helps swelling go down and stops it stiffening.
setup: Sit with your leg supported and the foot free to move.
cues: Draw the alphabet with your big toe
feel: Easy movement in the ankle.
stopIf: Sharp pain.

name: Ankle outward push (isometric)
why: Works the muscles on the outside of the ankle (peroneals) that protect against rolling it again, without moving the sore joint.
setup: Sit with the outside of the foot against a wall or table leg.
cues: Push the outside of your foot out
mistakes: Turning the knee instead of the foot
feel: Effort along the outside of the ankle and lower leg.
stopIf: Sharp pain.

name: Resisted ankle eversion (band)
why: Strengthens the outside-ankle muscles through their full movement, one of the keys to avoiding repeat sprains.
setup: Sit with legs straight. Loop a band round the working forefoot and anchor it to the inside (round the other foot).
cues: Turn the sole of your foot outwards
feel: Work along the outside of the ankle and shin.
stopIf: Sharp ankle pain.

name: Single-leg balance on a cushion
why: Balancing on a soft surface trains the fast reactions that stop an ankle rolling. Balance training clearly reduces repeat ankle sprains.
setup: Stand on one leg on a folded towel, pillow or cushion, near a wall or counter.
cues: Let the ankle make small corrections
Eyes closed for a harder version
mistakes: Grabbing the wall all the time
feel: Small muscles round the ankle and hip working hard.
stopIf: Ankle pain or giving way.

name: Single-leg hops
why: Small hops on one leg prepare the ankle, calf and knee for running and sport. A good test that you're ready to return.
setup: Stand on one leg with space around you.
feel: Springy work in the calf and ankle.
stopIf: Pain, or the ankle or knee feels unstable.
